claims.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit intrinsic heterogeneous lattice strain at temperatures of at least 1000 °C.
Elevated temperature triggers heterogeneous lattice strain in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Heterogeneous lattice strain causes unusual dislocation behaviors, including multiple kinks, jogs, and bidirectional cross slips.
Localized lattice misfit drives the activation and evolution of kink, jog, and cross-slip dislocation structures.
Lattice distortion can affect mechanical deformation by restricting expansion of the plastic zone.
Strain-induced unusual dislocation behavior contributes to mechanical strengthening.
The strain-induced dislocation mechanisms control high-temperature creep resistance.
The strain-induced dislocation mechanisms control thermoelastic response by changing local stress fields and energy dissipation.
Compared with a material having more uniform lattice characteristics, a heterogeneously strained refractory HEA will exhibit more multiple kinks, jogs, and bidirectional cross slips.
Compared with the baseline, a heterogeneously strained refractory HEA will have improved creep resistance.
Compared with the baseline, a heterogeneously strained refractory HEA will have a distinct thermoelastic response.
A controlled comparison should use alloys of similar composition that differ in their degree of intrinsic lattice strain.
High-temperature in-situ neutron diffraction, creep measurements, and post-test microscopy can be combined to compare lattice strain, dislocation structures, creep rate, and thermoelastic response.
Consistent atmospheres should be used at high temperature to minimize oxidation effects.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at lower temperatures or when significant secondary phases form.
Equivalent dislocation activity, creep response, and thermoelastic response in high-strain and low-strain alloys would falsify the proposed governing role of heterogeneous lattice strain.
